clue.text: Frank works in a gallery, retired in a sense

indicators.note: To retire is to withdraw, going back the way you came, so the letters beside it are written the other way round.

parts.note: one of the five senses, and this word parts after its first letter to take another piece in
the works hanging in a gallery are art, arriving back to front

explanation.walkthrough: 'Frank' looks like the name of the man who works in the gallery, and it is the definition standing at the front of the clue all along.
explanation.definitionFit: Frank -> STRAIGHT: a straight answer is an honest and direct one, the plain-dealing sense of the word rather than anything about lines.

clue.text: Fool admits going round new places sharing culture

indicators.note: What goes round another thing closes about it, so the fool's letters wrap themselves about the single letter named next.

parts.note: a twit is a fool, and these four letters open after the third
n is the standard abbreviation for new, as on a product label
to admit to a thing is to own up to it

explanation.walkthrough: 'Admits' is placed to look like the instruction to put something inside, and it is a piece of the answer in its own right; a different phrase does the enclosing.
explanation.definitionFit: places sharing culture -> TWIN TOWNS: a town formally paired with one abroad, swapping school visits and festivals with it, is its twin town.

clue.text: Nurse fish with twisted tail

indicators.note: Something twisted has been wrenched round to face the other way, so the letters it points at are read in reverse.

parts.note: to fish is to angle, and the first three letters of that verb stay as they are
the tail of that same verb is its last two letters, which arrive the other way round

explanation.walkthrough: 'Fish' is a verb here, the sport of angling, not a creature — and the setter is enjoying the fact that the answer names a fish too.
explanation.definitionFit: Nurse -> ANGEL: nurses have been called angels since Florence Nightingale, the affectionate name for anyone who tends the sick.

clue.text: Get everything out of tower that's going up

indicators.note: This entry runs down the grid, so letters going up are read from the bottom square towards the top.

parts.note: a tug tows barges and liners, so it is a tower — nothing to do with buildings

explanation.walkthrough: 'Tower' wants to be something tall with a spire on it. The small boat that does the towing is the reading that fits, and it is one of the oldest dodges in the crossword.
explanation.definitionFit: Get everything out of -> GUT: to gut a fish or a building is to strip out everything inside and leave only the shell.

clue.text: Hard, taking hour from start to finish

indicators.note: To take something in is to receive it inside yourself, so the piece named next is planted within the word before it.

parts.note: a hard problem is a tough one, and this word splits after its first letter
hr is the abbreviation printed on a timetable

explanation.walkthrough: The comma after 'Hard' makes it look like a remark aimed at the solver, so the definition seems to have started already. It is the wordplay, and the definition is the phrase at the end.
explanation.definitionFit: from start to finish -> THROUGH: reading a book through means going the whole way from the first page to the last without stopping.

clue.text: Only son with acne wanting face wiped

indicators.note: A word described as wanting is short of something it ought to have, so a piece of it is missing.
Wiped means rubbed clean off the slate, which is what happens to the letter this acts on.

parts.note: s is the genealogist's abbreviation for son
someone with acne is pimply, and that word turns up here with its front letter gone
the face of a word is the letter at its front, and this is the one that goes

explanation.walkthrough: 'Only son' reads as one phrase about a family, and its two words belong to opposite halves of the clue: one is the definition, the other a single letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Only -> SIMPLY: in the sense of merely — 'I simply asked' and 'I only asked' play down what was done in exactly the same way.

clue.text: Somewhat inexpert heads of Spectre each botched assassinations?

indicators.note: The head of a word is the letter standing at its front, so each name after this gives up its opening letter.

parts.note: the opening letter of each of these two words, taken in the order they stand
killings carried out badly, using the prefix MIS- that English puts in front of anything done wrongly

explanation.walkthrough: Two traps in one clue: 'Somewhat' usually announces a hidden word and here belongs to the definition, and 'botched' shuffles nothing — it builds a MIS- word.
explanation.definitionFit: Somewhat inexpert -> SEMISKILLED: a semi-skilled worker has had some training but no full trade, so their competence stops short of expert.

clue.text: Guy silences husky relatives

parts.note: a guy is a male, the man rather than the rope holding a tent up
to silence a sound is to mute it

explanation.walkthrough: 'Husky' sits there as an adjective describing a hoarse guy, and it is the dog. The breed is more often spelt malamute; both spellings are in the dictionaries.
explanation.definitionFit: husky relatives -> MALEMUTES: these Alaskan sled dogs come of the same northern spitz stock as huskies, so the definition names them as kin.

clue.text: Estate Volvo's unique character, alongside Sierra

definitions.note: An estate is one holding while the answer is plural: English has long spoken of a family's lands as the single property they own.

parts.note: the only letter appearing once in VOLVO, since the V and the O each turn up twice
putting one thing alongside another is putting this and that together
S in the NATO alphabet, where each letter has a name that carries over a radio

explanation.walkthrough: Volvo and Sierra are both cars and an estate is a body style, so the whole surface is a forecourt. Not one of those three words is doing what it appears to.
explanation.definitionFit: Estate -> LANDS: a country estate is the ground a family owns, and lands is the collective word for precisely that holding.

clue.text: Wee half-way through good Spielberg film

parts.note: the point half-way through anything is its mid-point
g is the standard abbreviation for good, as on a school report
E.T. is the Spielberg film of 1982 about the stranded alien

explanation.walkthrough: 'Wee' is Scots for tiny, the sense wanted rather than the nursery one. E.T. is worth remembering: the crossword's favourite two-letter film.
explanation.definitionFit: Wee -> MIDGET: wee means very small, and midget carries the same sense as an adjective — a midget submarine, a midget car.

clue.text: King on walkabout making little sense

parts.note: R is rex, Latin for king, the letter a monarch signs after their name
somebody on a walkabout is ambling about at an easy pace

explanation.walkthrough: A royal walkabout is a real fixture of British life, which is what makes 'King' look like part of the picture rather than a single letter of wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: making little sense -> RAMBLING: speech that wanders off in all directions and arrives nowhere is described as rambling.

clue.text: Where we live, every hotel opens annoyingly late

indicators.note: Something that opens comes apart to let another thing in, so the phrase beside it splits and takes the pieces named inside.

parts.note: 'at ours' is the everyday British way of saying at our place — come back to ours — and it parts in the middle
every one of them is all of them
H is hotel in the NATO alphabet

explanation.walkthrough: 'Where we live' wants to be a country or a street name. It is the colloquial phrase instead, and 'hotel' is a letter rather than a building.
explanation.definitionFit: annoyingly late -> AT ALL HOURS: somebody who comes home at all hours turns up at any hour of the night, the phrase always carrying a complaint.

clue.text: Sorting out her hair and mood, a pain in the arse?

indicators.note: Sorting a heap out means putting it into a fresh arrangement, which is exactly what becomes of these letters.

parts.note: eleven letters handed over whole, in an order that will not survive

explanation.walkthrough: The surface is a hairdresser soothing a difficult client, and the definition is that idiom taken absolutely literally — which is what the question mark owns up to.
explanation.definitionFit: a pain in the arse -> HAEMORRHOID: the idiom for a maddening nuisance, read at its word, since this swollen vein really does hurt there.

clue.text: Wish you were with younger woman?

definitions.meaning: the verb: to feel somebody's absence and want them back
the courtesy title put before an unmarried woman's name, and the noun for a girl

explanation.walkthrough: The first half is quoting the postcard — wish you were here — and the two halves run on as one sentence, with nothing at all marking the seam between them.
explanation.definitionFit: Wish you were -> MISS is to feel the absence of somebody; younger woman -> MISS is the title an unmarried woman is addressed by.

clue.text: Noel made pretty clever electronics during joint postgrad courses

indicators.note: What happens during something happens inside it, so the piece named before this goes within the word that follows.

parts.note: the joint at the base of your hand, and it opens after its first letter
clever electronics are hi-tech, the two halves run together
MAs are Master of Arts degrees, courses taken after a first degree

explanation.walkthrough: The surface has electronics students on a joint degree. The joint wanted is the one in your arm, and what makes a Noel pretty is snow.
explanation.definitionFit: Noel made pretty -> WHITE CHRISTMAS: a Christmas under snow is the prettified version everybody sings about, so the phrase names Noel dressed up.

clue.text: Wrong since exposed by cycling clergyman

indicators.note: a word exposed has had its covering stripped away, so its first and last letters go

parts.note: the word whose inner letters are kept

indicators.note: the letters of the clergyman go round, some moving from the front to the back

parts.note: a rector is a parish clergyman

explanation.surface: Something has been wrong ever since a cleric on a bicycle was caught out.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Exposed' strips the outer letters of 'since', leaving INC. 'Cycling' rotates RECTOR so that its first two letters, RE, move to the end, giving ORRECT.
explanation.definitionFit: Incorrect is the plain synonym of wrong: mistaken, not true.

clue.text: Attacked when seconds at duel ordered

indicators.note: To order a set of things is to arrange them, and letters put into a fresh arrangement come out spelling something else.

parts.note: as means when — 'as I arrived' is 'when I arrived'
s stands for second in any timing, and setters use it for the plural as readily as the singular
six more letters, the clue's own words taken exactly as they stand

explanation.walkthrough: A duel's seconds are the friends who attend the duellists and check the pistols, which is why the surface reads as a scene rather than a heap of letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Attacked -> ASSAULTED: the legal and everyday word for a physical attack on a person, matching the clue's past tense exactly.

clue.text: Doctor says no physical treatment for problems

indicators.note: To doctor something is to tamper with it, and letters tampered with come out in a different order.

parts.note: fourteen letters handed over, the full length of the entry

explanation.walkthrough: 'Doctor' at the head of a medical surface is doing the shuffling rather than attending anybody, and the treatment defined is the talking kind, with nothing physical about it.
explanation.definitionFit: treatment for problems -> PSYCHOANALYSIS: Freud's method of treating mental trouble by talking through what the patient has buried, so the problems are those of the mind.

clue.text: Nervous about Tesla's gearbox position breaking transmission

indicators.note: A thing set about another is wrapped round it, so the word beside this closes over the letter that follows.

parts.note: nervous in the anatomical sense, of the nerves, and this word opens after its third letter
T is the symbol for the tesla, the unit of magnetic field strength

explanation.walkthrough: Everything in the surface is a car — Tesla, gearbox, transmission — and the one word doing wordplay is 'nervous', in its medical rather than its anxious sense.
explanation.definitionFit: gearbox position breaking transmission -> NEUTRAL: with the box in neutral no gear is engaged, so the drive from engine to wheels is disconnected.

clue.text: Broadcast beginning with piano duet

indicators.note: What a thing begins with stands at its front, so the letter named here is written before the rest.

parts.note: p is the mark in a score telling the player to play softly, from the Italian
to broadcast a programme is to air it

explanation.walkthrough: 'Broadcast' is exactly the sort of word that announces a homophone, and here it is a plain synonym. The piano is a marking on sheet music, not the instrument.
explanation.definitionFit: duet -> PAIR: two performing together are a pair, the definition naming the answer by one particular kind of twosome.

clue.text: Secretary brought over card with dispatch

indicators.note: Bringing something over turns it round to face the other way, so those letters are read in reverse.

parts.note: a PA is a personal assistant, the office secretary, and the pair arrives the other way round
the ace is the highest card in the pack

explanation.walkthrough: 'With dispatch' looks like a link phrase — sent off with something — and it is the definition. Dispatch here means promptness, a sense that survives mainly in this phrase.
explanation.definitionFit: with dispatch -> APACE: to do a thing apace is to do it quickly, and dispatch in its older sense means exactly that promptness.

clue.text: With diversions, outdo urban one-way system

indicators.note: A diversion sends traffic off its proper route, and letters sent off their route arrive in a different order.

parts.note: ten letters handed over, exactly the length of the entry

explanation.walkthrough: The whole surface is traffic management, which hides the fact that two ordinary words are simply being taken to pieces. 'Outdo' is the last word you would think to shuffle.
explanation.definitionFit: one-way system -> ROUNDABOUT: traffic on a roundabout circulates one way round the island, so the junction is a one-way system in miniature.

clue.text: Child in Scotland showing AI lowered mental ability

indicators.note: AI is the pair of letters being worked on, not an instruction, and lowered means further down the column in a down entry — so that pair slides down the word and the rest closes up above it.

parts.note: a bairn is a child in Scots, the everyday word north of the border

explanation.walkthrough: Nothing is jumbled at random: the two letters named move down two places in the column and everything above them shuffles up to fill the gap.
explanation.definitionFit: mental ability -> BRAIN: having brain, or brains, is the informal way of saying you have the intelligence a job needs.

clue.text: Attendee at meeting developing career, full of pep

indicators.note: A developing thing changes shape as it goes, so these letters do not keep the arrangement they were handed in.
Something full of a thing has it inside, so the short piece goes into the middle of the letters just rearranged.

parts.note: six letters handed over to be reordered
go is pep or energy — there is plenty of go in him

explanation.walkthrough: 'Meeting' is the racing sense, a day's card of races at one course, and 'developing career' is an appraisal-form phrase quietly doing letter work.
explanation.definitionFit: Attendee at meeting -> RACEGOER: a race meeting is a fixture at a course, and the people who turn up for it are racegoers.

clue.text: Modest expedition led by Conservative

indicators.note: Whatever leads goes in front, so the letter named after this is written before the rest.

parts.note: C is the standard abbreviation for the Conservative party on a ballot paper
expedition in its old sense of speed — doing a thing with expedition is doing it fast

explanation.walkthrough: 'Expedition' looks like a journey and means promptness, the sense that survives in 'expedite'. The surface is a Tory-led trek and neither half of it is true.
explanation.definitionFit: Modest -> CHASTE: chaste means pure and restrained, and by extension plain and unadorned — the modest sense of dress or taste.

clue.text: Turning and pushing piece starts to annoy Magnus Carlsen terribly

indicators.note: The start of a word is the letter it begins with, so each name after this gives up its first letter only.
Something done terribly is done badly, and letters handled badly end up out of their proper order.

parts.note: the letter that begins each of these three words, taken in the order they stand

explanation.walkthrough: Magnus Carlsen is the world chess champion, which is what makes 'piece' read as a chessman. The piece defined is a piece of machinery.
explanation.definitionFit: Turning and pushing piece -> CAM: a cam is the lobed wheel on a spinning shaft whose bulge shoves a follower, turning rotation into a shove.

clue.text: Angry husband very happy when learner driver vanishes

indicators.note: Something that vanishes is simply not there any more, so the letter named beside it never joins the word.

parts.note: H is the standard abbreviation for husband, as on a form
very happy is elated, and that word arrives with its L missing
the L-plate a learner driver carries, and this is the letter that goes

explanation.walkthrough: The surface is a husband delighted to see the back of a learner on the road, which keeps the deletion out of sight; the definition is a single word at the front.
explanation.definitionFit: Angry -> HEATED: a heated exchange is a furious one, the metaphor of temper as temperature that English uses everywhere.

clue.text: Article in French newspaper that's refreshingly sharp

indicators.note: A thing said to be in another sits within it, so the letter named first is planted inside the name that follows.

parts.note: Le Monde is the Paris daily, its title the French for 'the world'
the indefinite article, which in wordplay is simply the letter

explanation.walkthrough: 'Article in French' wants to be LE, the French for 'the'. The article here is the English one, and it goes inside the newspaper's title.
explanation.definitionFit: that's refreshingly sharp -> LEMONADE: the drink is sharp with lemon and served cold to cool you down, so the phrase describes it by taste.
